usage: 알 is the natural market counter for round fruit; 한 알 sounds more grocer-like than 한 개.
A genuinely common allergy here; memorize this exact phrase for restaurants and friends' homes.
Do you buy soft peaches or firm ones?
물복(물렁한 복숭아) vs 딱복(딱딱한 복숭아) — the camp question Koreans really ask each other.
Adjective 무르다 → past 물렀다; peaches bruise and over-soften fast, so this comes up often.
examples: 복숭아 좋아해요?
Do you like peaches?
Simplest frame — just the noun + 좋아하다, no counter or particle traps yet.
여름 되면 복숭아가 진짜 맛있어요.
When summer comes, peaches are really delicious.
되면 = 'when it becomes'; marks 복숭아 as a signature summer fruit.
저는 딱복은 별로고 물복이 좋아요.
I'm not big on firm peaches; I like the soft juicy ones.
Real preference talk: 별로다 (not great) contrasted with 좋다, using the slang short forms.
nuance: 복숭아 is a native Korean word (no hanja) for one of the country's most beloved summer fruits, and it carries real cultural weight: people genuinely split into two camps, 물복 (soft, juicy 물렁복숭아) versus 딱복 (firm, crunchy 딱딱한 복숭아), and asking which someone prefers is small talk. The nearest confusion for learners is texture verbs: when a peach over-softens you say 물렀어요 (from 무르다, to go soft), NOT 썩었어요 (rotten) — mixing those up makes a perfectly good peach sound spoiled. It is also one of Korea's most common food allergies, so 복숭아 알레르기 있어요 is a high-value safety phrase. English speakers often reach for 개 as the counter, but at a fruit stand 한 알 (for one round piece) is far more natural; 개 isn't wrong, just less grocer-like.

mistakes: Counting 복숭아 with 개 at a market — for round fruit a vendor expects 한 알; 개 sounds like you're counting generic objects, not produce.
Saying 복숭아가 썩었어요 (rotten) when you only mean it's overripe and soft — the correct word is 물렀어요, from the adjective 무르다.
Treating 물복/딱복 as childish slang to avoid — they're the standard everyday terms; using 물렁한 복숭아 every time sounds stiff.

usage: One bag of Korean melons, please
Often priced by the 봉지 (mesh bag) at markets and marts, not by the single piece.
We peel and eat Korean melon
깎다 = to peel/pare with a knife; the yellow skin comes off first.
Seongju chamoe is the most famous
성주 (a county in 경북) is the gold-standard growing region, like a brand of origin.
The yellow ones are the tasty ones
게 = 것이; ripe 참외 turns bright yellow with pale ridged stripes.
examples: 참외 처음 봐요.
I'm seeing chamoe for the first time.
Beginner frame: 처음 보다 = to see for the first time, perfect for this very local fruit.
여름에 참외 깎아서 냉장고에 넣어 두면 시원해요.
In summer, peel chamoe and chill it in the fridge.
넣어 두다 = put it in and leave it; -아 두다 means doing something in advance for later.
이 참외 진짜 달다, 한번 먹어 봐.
This chamoe is really sweet, try a piece.
Casual 반말: plain 달다 + the offer 먹어 봐 (try eating), how you'd talk to a close friend.
nuance: 참외 is the bright-yellow oriental melon that is almost unknown outside Korea, which makes it a delightfully local word to own. Etymology helps it stick: 참 means 'true/real' (as in 참기름 'real sesame oil') and 외 is the old word for melon/gourd, so 참외 is literally 'the genuine melon.' The single biggest learner trap is translating it as 'melon' and saying 멜론 — but 멜론 in Korean means the imported netted cantaloupe/honeydew, a totally different fruit; 참외 is its own category and should stay 참외. Unlike a watermelon you slice into wedges, 참외 is 깎아 먹는 (peeled) fruit: you pare off the yellow skin, and many people scoop out the soft seedy core too. The 성주 region functions like an origin label the way certain places are famous for specific produce, so '성주 참외' signals premium.

Eating 참외 with the peel on — Koreans pare off the yellow skin first (깎아 먹다); leaving it on reads as not knowing how to eat it.
Saying 참외 한 개 at a market when it's bagged — it's commonly sold and counted by the 봉지 (bag), so 한 봉지 fits the real buying unit.

usage: Counted with 알 like other small round fruit; -ㄹ래? is a casual offer/invitation.
새콤하다 = pleasantly, refreshingly sour — a positive word, unlike harsh 시다.
Plums are in season right now
제철 (제 + 철, 'its own season') = peak season, roughly June–July.
씨 = seed/pit; you bite the flesh around the hard central stone.
examples: 자두 새콤해요.
Plums are tart.
Two-word frame fixing the core flavor adjective 새콤하다 to the fruit.
자두는 씻어서 통째로 먹으면 돼요.
Just wash the plums and eat them whole.
통째로 = whole/in one piece; -으면 돼요 = 'it's fine if you just…', the easy default.
마트에 자두 나온 거 보니까 여름 다 됐네.
Seeing plums out at the mart, summer's basically here.
-(으)니까 here = 'now that I see…, I realize'; 보니까 (from 보다) frames seasonal fruit as a season signal.
nuance: 자두 is a small, tart-sweet stone fruit (native Korean word, no hanja) piled high at markets from around June, and the flavor Koreans reach for is 새콤달콤 — a fixed pair meaning 'pleasantly sour-and-sweet.' Note the synonym line in that word: 새콤하다 is the GOOD kind of sour (refreshing, appetizing), whereas plain 시다 is just 'sour' and can sound like a complaint, and 떫다 is the puckery astringency of unripe persimmon — don't swap them. Unlike 복숭아, you normally eat 자두 통째로 (whole, skin on), just biting around the hard central 씨 (pit), so peeling it like a peach marks you as unfamiliar with it. The classic learner mix-up is sound-based: 자두 (plum) vs 자몽 (grapefruit) — one syllable apart but entirely different fruit, so listen for the 두/몽 ending.

mistakes: Confusing 자두 (plum) with 자몽 (grapefruit) — they sound alike but are unrelated; the second syllable (두 vs 몽) is the whole difference.
Peeling 자두 like a peach — the thin skin is eaten as-is; you simply wash it and eat it 통째로 (whole), biting around the pit.
Using 시다 for the nice tang — for ripe plum say 새콤하다 (appetizingly sour); 시다 alone can sound like the fruit is too sour to enjoy.

usage: Want a firm persimmon or a soft one?
단감 (crunchy, eaten like an apple) vs 홍시 (soft, jelly-like, spooned) — name the type, not just 감.
떫다 = puckery/mouth-drying — the signature word for an underripe 감, not 'bitter.'
곶감 = peeled, dried persimmon; a chewy, very sweet winter treat eaten as a snack.
Counted with 개; 따다 = to pick from the tree, since 감 grows on backyard trees.
examples: 가을엔 감이 달아요.
In autumn persimmons are sweet.
Short seasonal frame: 가을엔 (in autumn) + 달다 (sweet).
저는 딱딱한 단감을 더 좋아해요.
I prefer the firm, crunchy persimmon.
더 좋아하다 = to prefer (like more); 단감 is the apple-crisp variety.
덜 익은 감은 떫어서 입에 못 대요.
Unripe persimmons are so astringent I can't touch them.
입에 대다 = to put to one's mouth/taste; 못 대다 = can't even try it, vivid spoken phrasing.
nuance: 감 is the quintessential autumn fruit (native Korean, no hanja), and crucially it is an umbrella word that splits into named forms: 단감 (literally 'sweet 감,' the firm crunchy kind eaten sliced like an apple), 홍시 (紅枾 'red persimmon,' the soft jelly-like ripe one you scoop with a spoon), and 곶감 (peeled and dried into a chewy sweet for winter). At a market, saying just 감 is vague — sellers and friends specify which. The flavor word every learner must nail is 떫다 (astringent): an unripe persimmon dries out your whole mouth, and English speakers wrongly call this 써요 (bitter) — but 쓰다 is coffee-bitter, while 떫다 is the puckery tannin sensation, a different word entirely. So 감이 떫어요, never 감이 써요.

mistakes: Using bare 감 when you mean a specific kind — at a market specify 단감 (firm) or 홍시 (soft); 감 alone is ambiguous about texture.
Saying 감이 써요 (bitter) for an unripe one — the correct sensation is 떫다 (astringent); 쓰다 means bitter like coffee, a different taste.
Assuming 곶감 is just 'dried fruit' — it specifically means peeled-and-dried persimmon and is treated as a sweet/snack, not a substitute for fresh 감.

usage: 망고 빙수 (mango shaved ice) is the flagship summer café dessert; -으러 가다 = go in order to.
익다 = to ripen; a ripe 망고 is soft to the touch and fragrant.
냉동 (冷凍 'cold-freeze') = frozen; the budget way to buy it, sold in bags for smoothies.
Apple mango is a bit pricey
애플망고 = the small, deep-orange premium variety, sold and priced apart from regular 망고.
examples: 망고 좋아해요?
Do you like mango?
Plain noun + 좋아하다, the simplest opener.
망고는 좀 비싸지만 가끔 사 먹어요.
Mango's a bit pricey, but I buy it once in a while.
-지만 = 'but' (concession); 사 먹다 = buy-and-eat, the natural verb for treating yourself.
여름에 카페에서 망고 빙수 한 그릇 먹으면 천국이에요.
A bowl of mango bingsu at a café in summer is heaven.
그릇 = bowl-counter for 빙수; -으면 …이에요 frames the payoff.
nuance: 망고 is a loanword (from English 'mango') and, importantly, it carries a 'special imported treat' connotation that the English word lacks — because it's pricier and not locally grown, it reads as an occasional indulgence rather than an everyday fruit like 사과 or 귤. Its single most famous form is 망고 빙수 (mango shaved ice), the dessert that defines summer café menus, so the collocation is worth memorizing as a unit. The key distinction learners miss: 망고 and 애플망고 are NOT interchangeable — 애플망고 is the smaller, sweeter, deep-orange premium type, separately labeled and noticeably more expensive, so don't expect them at the same price. For home use, 냉동 망고 (frozen, 冷凍) is the affordable everyday option people blend into smoothies, while fresh 망고 stays a small luxury.

Saying 망고 빙수 만들어요 to mean ordering it out — for café desserts you 먹으러 가다 (go to eat) or 시키다 (order); 만들다 implies making it yourself at home.

usage: Sold in small 팩 (plastic punnets), never loose — so the buying unit is 한 팩, not 한 개.
냉동 (冷凍) = frozen; the cheaper, year-round option versus pricey fresh 생블루베리.
Blueberries are good for your eyes
눈에 좋다 = good for the eyes; a near-universal health belief you'll hear repeated constantly.
A staple flavor for the yogurt bowls and smoothies popular with health-minded 20–30s.
examples: 블루베리 좀 사 왔어요.
I bought some blueberries.
사 오다 = buy-and-bring(-back); the everyday 'I picked some up' verb.
아침에 요거트에 블루베리 넣어 먹어요.
In the morning I add blueberries to my yogurt.
에 marks the destination (into the yogurt); 넣어 먹다 = add-and-eat, a habitual breakfast.
생블루베리는 비싸서 그냥 냉동으로 사요.
Fresh blueberries are pricey, so I just buy frozen.
생- prefix = raw/fresh (생블루베리); -아서 gives the reason for the practical choice.
nuance: 블루베리 is a loanword (from English 'blueberry') that in Korea is framed above all as a health food, not just a fruit — you will constantly hear 블루베리가 눈에 좋아요 ('good for your eyes'), and it anchors the yogurt-bowl-and-smoothie routine of health-conscious 20–30s. Two practical things shape how you talk about it. First, the counter: it's bought in small pricey 팩 (punnets), so the unit is 한 팩, and counting the whole container with 개 sounds off. Second, the fresh-vs-frozen split: 생블루베리 (생- = raw/fresh) is expensive, so many default to cheaper 냉동 (冷凍, frozen) bags — naming which one you mean matters at the store. Spelling pitfall for English speakers: the standard transliteration is 블루베리, NOT 블루배리 — the third syllable is 베, mirroring 'berry,' even though Korean ㅔ/ㅐ sound nearly identical.

mistakes: Counting the container with 개 — buy it as 한 팩 (one punnet); 개 would mean individual berries, which isn't how it's sold.
Spelling it 블루배리 — the correct loanword is 블루베리 (베, not 배); the ㅔ/ㅐ contrast is silent in speech but fixed in writing.
Assuming fresh is the norm — many people buy 냉동 (frozen) because 생블루베리 is expensive, so specify 생 vs 냉동 when it matters.

usage: 골드키위 (sweeter, premium) vs 그린키위 (tarter) — labeled and priced separately at the mart.
Counted with 개; 깎다 = to pare off the fuzzy brown skin with a knife.
Scooping kiwi out is the easy way
떠먹다 (뜨다 'scoop' + 먹다) = halve it and spoon out the flesh — a very common local habit.
시큼하다 = sharply sour; green kiwi that isn't ripe yet has a real tang.
examples: 키위 맛있어요.
Kiwi is tasty.
Bare noun + 맛있다 — the no-frills starter sentence.
키위는 반으로 잘라서 숟가락으로 떠먹어요.
I halve the kiwi and scoop it with a spoon.
반으로 자르다 = cut in half; -아서 chains the steps (cut, then scoop).
골드키위는 비싼데 그래도 그게 더 맛있어요.
Gold kiwi's pricey, but still, it tastes better.
-는데 sets up contrast; 그게 = 그것이, pointing back to the gold one.
nuance: 키위 is a loanword (from English 'kiwi') and an everyday, affordable fruit in Korea, but learners need to know it isn't one uniform thing: it splits into 골드키위 (gold, sweeter, premium, smoother-skinned) and 그린키위 (green, tarter), and these are shelved and priced as distinct items — assuming they taste the same is a real mistake. Two eating habits shape the vocabulary. You can 깎아 먹다 (peel and eat) like other fruit, but a signature Korean move is to halve it and 떠먹다 — 뜨다 'to scoop' + 먹다 — spooning the flesh straight out of the skin cup. The fuzzy brown skin is never eaten; reaching to eat it whole, skin and all, marks unfamiliarity. For flavor, underripe green kiwi is 시큼하다 (sharply sour) — distinguish this from 새콤하다, which is the pleasant refreshing sourness of ripe fruit.

usage: 데치다 = to blanch briefly in boiling water (not fully boil) — the standard prep here.
I buy one head of broccoli
송이 = the counter for a head/cluster/floret bunch; 개 doesn't fit a whole head.
살짝 = lightly/just a touch; keeps the broccoli green and crunchy instead of mushy.
We dip broccoli in chili-vinegar paste
초고추장 (초 醋 'vinegar' + 고추장) = the sweet-tangy red dip standard for blanched veg.
examples: 브로콜리 안 좋아해요.
I don't like broccoli.
Negation 안 + 좋아하다 — the simplest way to state a dislike.
브로콜리는 살짝 데쳐서 초고추장에 찍어 먹어요.
Blanch broccoli lightly and dip it in chili-vinegar sauce.
데치다 + 초고추장 is the classic combo; -아서 chains blanch → dip → eat.
브로콜리를 너무 오래 삶으면 물러져요.
If you boil broccoli too long, it gets mushy.
삶다 (full boil) contrasts with 데치다 (blanch); 물러지다 = to turn soft/mushy.
nuance: 브로콜리 is a loanword (from English 'broccoli') firmly tied to healthy and diet eating in Korea — it's a fixture on 닭가슴살 (chicken-breast) diet plates and 'clean eating' bowls, so the connotation leans 'health food,' not 'ordinary vegetable.' The most Korean way to serve it is 살짝 데친 (lightly blanched) and dipped in 초고추장, the sweet chili-vinegar paste; serving it raw and plain looks under-prepared by local norms. A crucial cooking-verb contrast for learners: 데치다 means to blanch briefly (just dunk it), while 삶다 means to fully boil — overdoing it (삶다 too long) makes the broccoli 물러지다 (go mushy), losing the crunch Koreans want. The counter trips people up too: a whole head is 한 송이 (the cluster counter), not 한 개, which would sound like you're tallying generic objects.

A crucial cooking-verb contrast: 데치다 means to blanch briefly (just dunk it), while 삶다 means to fully boil — overdoing it (삶다 too long) makes the broccoli 물러지다 (go mushy), losing the crunch Koreans want.
브로콜리 is a loanword from English 'broccoli'; 초고추장 combines 초 醋 'vinegar' + 고추장.

Counting it with 한 개 would sound like you're tallying generic objects; a whole head is 한 송이. And serving it raw and plain looks under-prepared by local norms — the expected style is blanched and dipped.

Serving 브로콜리 raw and plain — the expected style is 데친 (blanched) and dipped in 초고추장; raw looks under-prepared.
Confusing 데치다 with 삶다 — 데치다 is a quick blanch to keep it crunchy, while 삶다 (long boil) makes it 물러지다 (mushy).

usage: Sold in red, yellow, orange, and green; red is the sweetest, green the least sweet.
Counted with 개; 썰다 = to slice — it's firm and glossy, easy to cut into strips.
The headline fact: unlike 고추 (hot chili), 파프리카 is sweet and crunchy, zero heat.
I add bell pepper to salad
에 넣다 = add into; raw 파프리카 is a standard colorful, crunchy salad component.
examples: 파프리카 안 매워요.
Bell peppers aren't spicy.
Short reassurance frame fixing the single most important fact about 파프리카.
저는 파프리카 생으로 썰어서 그냥 먹어요.
I just slice bell peppers and eat them raw.
생으로 = raw/uncooked; -아서 chains slice → eat; 그냥 = 'just (as is).'
볶음 요리에 파프리카 넣으면 색깔이 예뻐요.
Adding bell pepper to a stir-fry makes the colors pretty.
볶음 요리 = stir-fry dish; often added for color and crunch as much as flavor.
nuance: 파프리카 is a loanword — but from Dutch 'paprika' (Korea imports the seeds/produce heavily from the Netherlands), which is why it isn't the English 'bell pepper.' The number-one thing for English speakers: 파프리카 is the sweet, NON-spicy bell pepper, totally distinct from 고추, the hot chili — assuming 'pepper = spicy' leads to real confusion at the table. There's a second, finer distinction Koreans make that learners flatten: 파프리카 vs 피망. 파프리카 is the large, thick-walled, sweet, glossy one in bright colors; 피망 (from French/Japanese 'piment') is the smaller, thinner, slightly bitter green pepper used in stir-fries — they're sold as separate items, so calling everything 파프리카 will occasionally be wrong. It's a major Korean export crop, so it's everywhere, affordable, and eaten 생으로 (raw) in salads or as crunchy snack strips, as well as added to stir-fries for color.

usage: We make and eat stir-fried eggplant
볶음 = stir-fry; 가지볶음 is a common 반찬 (side dish), 해 먹다 = make-and-eat at home.
나물 = steamed-then-seasoned vegetable side; 가지나물 is soft, savory, sesame-dressed.
Counted with 개; Korean 가지 is the long, slender purple kind, not the round Western one.
물컹하다 = soft and squishy — the cooked texture that decides who likes it.
examples: 저는 가지 못 먹어요.
I can't eat eggplant.
못 먹다 = can't eat (it's not for me) — a very common kid-and-adult line about 가지.
가지를 기름에 볶으면 부드러워져요.
When you stir-fry eggplant in oil, it gets tender.
기름에 볶다 = stir-fry in oil; -아지다 on 부드럽다 = 'becomes soft.'
가지나물은 호불호가 좀 갈려요.
Seasoned eggplant is a love-it-or-hate-it dish.
호불호가 갈리다 (好不好, 'like/dislike divides') = opinions split — a set idiom for polarizing foods.
nuance: 가지 in Korea means the long, slender, deep-purple eggplant, not the bulbous Western globe type, so picture a thinner shape. It's a native Korean word — and here's the pitfall that genuinely trips learners: 가지 is a homonym. The same 가지 also means 'kind/type/sort,' as in 한 가지 ('one kind'), 여러 가지 ('various kinds'), and it's even a noun for a tree branch — so context alone tells you whether someone means the vegetable or 'a type of.' As food, it lives mostly as two side dishes: 가지나물 (steamed then seasoned, soft) and 가지볶음 (stir-fried). Its soft 물컹한 texture makes it a textbook 호불호 (好不好, like-or-dislike) food, especially for kids, so it surfaces constantly in 'what foods do you hate?' conversations. Texture note: 물컹하다 (unpleasantly squishy) vs 부드럽다 (pleasantly tender) — same softness, opposite attitude, so choose by whether you mean it kindly.

usage: 군- (from 굽다 'to roast') = roasted; 군고구마 is the iconic winter street snack.
Give me one sweet potato, please
Counted with 개 or 하나; a everyday request at a stall or mart.
This drama is so frustrating (lit. 'so sweet-potato')
Slang: 고구마 = a stifling, no-payoff situation, like choking on dry sweet potato.
꿀- ('honey') = the moister, extra-sweet variety, versus the drier 밤고구마 ('chestnut').
examples: 고구마 좋아해요.
I like sweet potatoes.
Plain noun + 좋아하다 — and a word you'll hear daily in winter.
고구마는 다이어트할 때 밥 대신 먹기도 해요.
People sometimes eat sweet potato instead of rice when dieting.
밥 대신 = instead of rice; -기도 하다 = 'also (sometimes) do.'
그 드라마 너무 고구마라서 보다가 껐어.
That drama was so 'sweet potato' I turned it off mid-watch.
Slang in action: 고구마 + -라서 (because it's…); 보다가 껐어 = was watching, then shut it off.
nuance: 고구마 (native Korean word) is two things at once, and you need both. Literally it's the sweet potato — beloved as winter 군고구마 (군- 'roasted', from 굽다), and a favorite diet carb eaten 밥 대신 (instead of rice). Figuratively it's living slang: calling a drama, story, or situation 고구마 means it's frustrating and STIFLING — the image is choking on dry sweet potato with no water. Its built-in antonym is 사이다 (lit. cider/soda), the refreshing 'satisfying, cathartic' payoff; 20–30s constantly contrast a 고구마 (maddening) stretch with a 사이다 (gratifying) moment. Two pitfalls: don't confuse 고구마 with 감자 (regular potato) — different food and different slang weight (감자 has no such meaning); and don't take 고구마 같다 literally as being about food — it's an emotion word meaning 'so frustrating I could scream.' Variety note: 꿀고구마 (honey, moist-sweet) vs 밤고구마 (chestnut, drier-fluffy) are the two types people actually choose between.

mistakes: Confusing 고구마 (sweet potato) with 감자 (regular white potato) — different foods, and only 고구마 carries the 'frustrating' slang.

Treating all sweet potato as one — 꿀고구마 (moist, very sweet) and 밤고구마 (drier, fluffier like chestnut) are the named varieties Koreans pick between.

usage: I buy one steamed corn (on the cob)
찌다 → 찐 (steamed); 찐 옥수수 is a popular warm-weather street snack.
Counted with 개 for a cob — NOT 송이; 개 is the right counter here.
통조림 (통 'can' + 조림) = canned goods; canned corn goes in salads, on pizza, in 김밥.
옥수수차 = roasted-corn tea, a free table drink served hot or cold like 보리차.
examples: 옥수수 맛있어요.
Corn is tasty.
Bare noun + 맛있다 — the minimal starter sentence.
여름에 길에서 찐 옥수수 사 먹어요.
In summer I buy steamed corn from street stalls.
길에서 = on the street; 사 먹다 = buy-and-eat, the habitual snacking verb.
여기는 물 대신 옥수수차를 주네요.
Here they give corn tea instead of water.
물 대신 = instead of water; -네요 = mild noticing/remark about the free table tea.
nuance: 옥수수 (native Korean word) is corn, and the key for learners is that it reaches everyday life in three quite different forms, each with its own collocation: 찐 옥수수 (steamed on the cob, from 찌다 'to steam') as a summer street snack; 옥수수 통조림 (canned corn) sprinkled on salads, pizza, and into 김밥; and 옥수수차 (roasted-corn tea), poured free at many restaurants. That last one is the biggest trap: 옥수수차 is a brewed tea like 보리차 (barley tea), NOT a drink full of corn kernels — expecting kernels in your cup is the classic newcomer surprise. The counter also catches people: a cob is 한 개, never 한 송이 (송이 is for clusters/heads like broccoli or grapes), because a single cob counts as one object. So recognizing 찐 옥수수 / 옥수수 통조림 / 옥수수차 covers essentially everywhere you'll actually meet the word.
